newsitem.title: BELGIUM: INTERVIEW - L&H MOVES INTO INTERNET PRODUCTS.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - L&H MOVES INTO INTERNET PRODUCTS.

text.p: Belgium's Lernout & Hauspie Speech Products is moving into Internet products and services, entering an area that it regards as a major opportunity, L&H chairman Gaston Bastiaens told Reuters in a telephone interview.

The company, listed on the Nasdaq growth stocks market in the U.S., would use existing capabilities rather than set up a separate firm for these products which are to be ready in the first half of 1997, he said.
Bastiaens declined to give details on the expected contribution to turnover from the new products.
Currently, L&H does not sell own end-products, but has licence deals with major companies such as Microsoft and IBM to use its technology.

The new Internet products -- mainly software applications -- would in part be of the command/control type across a number of languages. They would, for instance, allow a user, speaking at normal speed, to tell a computer 'print this document' and the document would be printed.
"Eight languages are now ready as an engine," Bastiaens said. In the next six to nine months the number would be raised to 12, adding Chinese, Japanese, Arabic and Russian.
The applications should make the Internet more user-friendly and give a wider public access to the global information network.
"There are two main reasons why the Internet is not so successful in Europe...the telecommunications fees are too high...and...the language barrier," he said.
He was hopeful the fees would come down once the telecom market in Europe was liberalised in 1998.
The new products should help those who did not speak English use and explore the Internet where 90 percent of the information is in English.
The Internet services would focus on machine translation, using Brussels-based Mendez Translations, the firm L&H agreed to buy in September for $16.9 million.
Users would on the Internet send an electronic file to Mendez, which would produce a rough-cut, automatic, first translation, which if desired could later be refined by human hands, he said.
Bastiaens said L&H was in a unique position compared to its competitors because it offered products for other markets than purely the English language one.
He noted that Philips of the Netherlands had automated speech recognition products for the English and German market in specialist areas such as medicine and law.
IBM's products were mainly for the English language market, he added.
"We are clearly in market areas that are emerging, that will see substantial growth in the coming five to 10 years," he said.
L&H, set up in 1987, currently employs some 500 people. Its technology allows computers to recognise speech automatically, transform computer text into speech, or convert speech into digital signals.
It is available in a number of languages, including Dutch, French, German, Italian and Korean.
